newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU ministers to keep treaty review on track.
newsitem.headline: EU ministers to keep treaty review on track.

text.p: European Union foreign ministers will gather in the Netherlands on Sunday in a bid to step up the pace of wide-ranging reform talks ahead of a summit in Amsterdam in mid-June.

The Dutch EU presidency called the extra two-day ministerial session in the coastal resort of Noordwijk to inject fresh impetus into the inter-governmental conference (IGC) which began in Italy over a year ago.
There is a feeling that the IGC has been sidetracked by the high-profile run-up to economic and monetary union (EMU) and by attention given over to global trouble-spots such as Albania.

"There is maybe some concern and (Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo) has asked for more ministerial attention before this (feeling) changes into something worse," a Dutch foreign ministry spokesman said.

He said the IGC talks would continue along a twin track, with national representatives preparing the groundwork and ministers keeping the process on schedule for what is hoped will be a major review enshrined in a Treaty of Amsterdam at the June EU summit.
"It is quite clear now that we will accomplish something in Amsterdam. There is a good chance to have real reform and not to finish with something that has no real meaning."

Ministers, who got together less than two weeks ago in Rome to celebrate the bloc's 40th birthday, will be asked to focus on reviewing the Union's institutions which, many fear, could grind to a halt as the bloc expands eastwards over the next 10 years.
In an attempt to streamline policy-making, ministers will look at ways to trim the size of the executive European Commission and extend the scope of qualified majority voting.
But members remain divided over how a future Commission should look.

The 20-seat Commission has itself proposed slimming down to one seat per country, with a maximum of 20 as the EU expands. France, however, wants to wield the axe further, leaving a sleek, effective 10-seat body. But the bloc's smaller nations are loathe to surrender their national voice at the Brussels high-table.

On a more integrationist note, ministers will take another look at plans to incorporate the Western European Union (WEU), the bloc's fledgling defence club, into the EU, effectively creating a collective security policy and European army.
But the bloc's four neutral states, plus Britain, are unlikely to embrace a Franco-German-led plan for a phased move to a common defence policy.

With growing worker unrest across Europe and the biggest jobless figures in Germany since Hitler's rise to power, the EU is keen to signal to its 18 million unemployed that it cares about jobs by including an employment chapter in its social policy. But again, this is fiercely opposed by Britain's ruling Conservatives who fear the added costs for UK businesses.

Well-backed Dutch plans for immigration and asylum policy to be set at a European rather than national level are also likely to meet British resistance. Similarly, Britain and Ireland will demand an opt out from moves to extend the frontier-free Schengen agreement to the whole of the bloc.

But, as flexibility replaces federalism as the bloc's "F" buzz-word, the Dutch have garnered widespread support for a clause to allow some members to forge deeper integration without being slowed by the Euro-laggards.

The Dutch are up against a tight schedule to broker a revised treaty. If the IGC review is not finalised by the June summit, accession talks with those wanting to join the bloc will be delayed and risk becoming mired in crucial EMU decisions and French and German elections next year.
